blocks.text: One adrenal gland sits just above each kidney. Each has an inner adrenal medulla and an outer adrenal cortex. The medulla is controlled by the nervous system and the cortex by hormones of the anterior pituitary.

items: Adrenal medulla: epinephrine and norepinephrine (adrenaline and noradrenaline), released under stress to prepare the body for fight or flight: faster heart rate, higher blood pressure, wider bronchioles, higher blood glucose and less blood to the skin and digestive organs.

Adrenal cortex: the corticosteroids. Glucocorticoids such as cortisol keep glucose balance: they make muscle protein break down into amino acids, which the liver turns into glucose (gluconeogenesis). Mineralocorticoids such as aldosterone keep mineral balance: they make the kidneys reabsorb sodium, and water with it, keeping blood volume and pressure normal, and secrete excess potassium into the urine.

blocks.alt: Left: an oval islet of Langerhans surrounded by round exocrine acini; inside the islet many blue beta cells (insulin) and fewer red alpha cells (glucagon). Right: a cap-shaped adrenal gland on top of a dashed kidney, with a yellow outer cortex (cortisol, aldosterone) and a pink inner medulla (epinephrine, norepinephrine); a note says the medulla is controlled by nerves and the cortex by ACTH.
blocks.caption: The adrenal gland: cortex and medulla (original diagram after Figure 16.5).
blocks.long_description: Most of the pancreas is exocrine and makes pancreatic juice, but its islets of Langerhans are endocrine: the more numerous beta cells secrete insulin, which lowers blood glucose, and the alpha cells secrete glucagon, which raises it. Each adrenal gland has an outer cortex, which makes corticosteroids such as cortisol (glucose homeostasis) and aldosterone (salt and water balance) under the control of ACTH, and an inner medulla, which makes epinephrine and norepinephrine for the fight-or-flight response under nervous control.

items: Medulla: too much may cause hypertension and aggressive behaviour in daily life; too little leaves the body unable to cope with emergencies.

Cushing disease: too much cortisol, when the pituitary makes too much ACTH; excessive protein breakdown leads to high blood sugar, high blood pressure, thin bones, muscle loss, thin fragile skin, depression and excess facial hair in women.
Addison's disease: too little cortisol, with general metabolic disturbance, muscle weakness and loss of salts; the symptoms usually come on slowly.
